title: Pulse-by-pulse imaging of reversible, collective reshaping in laser-excited gold nanorods
authors: Mees Dieperink, Loriane Monin, Ichiro Ohnishi, Takeo Sasaki, Yu Jimbo, Erik Garnett, Wiebke Albrecht
abstract: Nanomaterial properties are governed by atomic structure, and driving structural changes on demand could enable materials with programmable properties. Pulsed light is the most controllable route: wavelength, fluence, polarization and pulse timing can each be tuned to inject energy with nanometre and picosecond precision and mould atomic positions. Yet the spatiotemporal dynamics of these transformations have remained hidden, inferred only from before-and-after snapshots. Here we track gold nanorods in a transmission electron microscope under pulsed optical excitation, quantifying the structural transition frame by frame. The rods enter an unexpectedly dynamic regime: material redistributes within and between particles, twin boundaries nucleate and propagate, rods hundreds of nanometres apart reshape in concert, and individual rods almost vanish before recovering their original shape, indicating a structural memory. Driving and following these transformations with pulse-synchronized in situ electron microscopy could turn light-induced reshaping into a tool for setting structure, and consequently properties, on demand.
summary: Researchers used pulse-synchronized in situ TEM to observe gold nanorods undergoing structural changes in real-time under pulsed laser excitation. They revealed a highly dynamic, correlated reshaping process exhibiting a structural memory. This technique establishes a new platform for controlling and understanding light-induced structural changes in nanomaterials.
main_problem: To resolve the spatiotemporal dynamics of structural transformations in nanomaterials driven by pulsed light, moving beyond simple before-and-after snapshots.
main_result: The system enters an unexpectedly dynamic regime exhibiting correlated, partly reversible restructuring, demonstrating a structural memory through repeated recovery of original shapes.
method: The study uses pulse-synchronized in situ Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) to capture structural snapshots frame-by-frame during pulsed optical excitation.
model_or_system: The physical system is gold nanorods (AuNRs) excited by a modulated CW laser tuned near the longitudinal Localized Surface Plasmon Resonance (LSPR). The analysis tracks structural changes like material redistribution and twin boundary nucleation.
key_observables: Structural state captured frame-by-frame, material redistribution, nucleation/propagation of twin boundaries, structural memory, and tip-asymmetry signal.
important_parameters: Peak temperature ($\sim 1115$ K), pulse duration ($400 \mu$s), and inter-pulse time ($40$ ms).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the cooling time is much shorter than the inter-pulse time, validating independent excitation events; volume change quantification is estimated from projected areas.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, pulse-resolved evolution of twinning and collective reorganization, and difference maps showing material gain or loss between pulses.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the novel pulse-synchronized TEM platform to detailing the observation of dynamic regimes, analyzing collective vs. isolated rod behavior, and finally comparing observed mass transport scales to theoretical diffusion limits.
why_interesting: The ability to resolve non-equilibrium structural dynamics event-by-event using pulsed light offers a powerful experimental tool for studying energy deposition and structural evolution in nanoscale systems, relevant to ultrafast energy transfer and phase transitions.
